name: Projectile range
seoDesc: Projectile range: work out horizontal velocity from the angle of launch and the range. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Projectile range calculator the angle of launch and the range and it returns horizontal velocity. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Projectile range calculator work?
sections.html:
The Projectile range calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports horizontal velocity in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the angle of launch and the range.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Projectile range calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Horizontal velocity=velocity × the cosine of (angle of launch)
Vertical velocity=velocity × the sine of (angle of launch)
Time of flight=range ÷ horizontal velocity
Horizontal velocity=the square root of ((velocity − vertical velocity) × (velocity + vertical velocity))
Time of flight=(20000 ÷ 196133) × vertical velocity + (200 ÷ 196133) × the square root of (196133 × initial height + 10000 × (vertical velocity ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Velocity = 10 m/s and Angle of launch = 10 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Horizontal velocity = 9.848 m/s and Vertical velocity = 1.736 m/s.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Horizontal velocity = 9.848 m/s and Vertical velocity = 1.736 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Velocity = 10 m/s and Angle of launch = 10 deg.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Length, opening in meters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Projectile range calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the angle of launch and the range — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Projectile range calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns horizontal velocity, derived from the angle of launch and the range. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Projectile range calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle of launch and the range, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter velocity in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Velocity opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Horizontal velocity = 9.848 m/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Projectile range calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
